title: About me
goal: Say who you are, where you're from and what languages you speak, and ask others the same.
intro:
This unit gives you the personal pronouns and the all-purpose 'is' word ആണ് *āṇŭ*. Here is the good news: **Malayalam verbs never change for the person**. 'I am', 'you are', 'she is', 'they are' are all just ആണ്.

You'll also meet the main question words. In speech, ആണ് is very often shortened to -ാ (-ā): എന്താണ് → എന്താ *endā* 'what is it?', ആരാണ് → ആരാ *ārā* 'who is it?'.

vocab.note: Object/oblique forms: എന്നെ (me), എനിക്ക് (to me), എന്റെ (my).
അവർ is also the polite way to refer to one older person.
ഇ- = near (this), അ- = far (that): ഇവൻ/അവൻ, ഇവൾ/അവൾ, ഇവർ/അവർ.
Negative: അല്ല. Colloquially shortened to -ാ: ഞാൻ ടീച്ചറാ.
'Where's your nāṭŭ?' is a standard getting-to-know-you question.
From അറിയുക 'to know'. Takes a dative subject: എനിക്ക് അറിയാം 'I know'.

phrases.en: My name is Anna. (lit. my name is 'Anna'-thus)

grammar.title: Pronouns and ആണ് 'is' — no person agreement!
grammar.body:
Malayalam pronouns:

ഞാൻ *ñān* I · ഞങ്ങൾ *ñaṅṅaḷ* we (not you) · നമ്മൾ *nammaḷ* we (incl. you)
നീ *nī* you (informal) · നിങ്ങൾ *niṅṅaḷ* you (polite/plural) · താങ്കൾ *tāṅgaḷ* you (formal)
അവൻ *avan* he · അവൾ *avaḷ* she · അത് *atŭ* it · അവർ *avar* they / he-she (respectful) · അദ്ദേഹം *addēham* he (very respectful)

The initial vowel shows distance: **ഇ-** = near (ഇവൻ 'this guy', ഇത് 'this'), **അ-** = far (അവൻ, അത്).

For 'X is Y' use **ആണ്** *āṇŭ* at the end. It **never changes**: ഞാൻ ... ആണ്, അവർ ... ആണ്. To say 'is not', replace ആണ് with **അല്ല** *alla*. In speech ആണ് often fuses with the word before it: ടീച്ചർ ആണ് → ടീച്ചറാണ് → ടീച്ചറാ.

grammar.title: Asking questions: question words and -ō
grammar.body:
**Question-word questions** keep normal word order; the question word usually goes right before the verb/ആണ്: നിങ്ങളുടെ പേര് **എന്താണ്**? 'Your name is what?'

Question words: എന്ത് *endŭ* what · ആര് *ārŭ* who · എവിടെ *eviṭe* where · എങ്ങനെ *eṅṅane* how · ഏത് *ētŭ* which · എപ്പോൾ *eppōḷ* when · എന്തിന് / എന്തുകൊണ്ട് why.

**Yes/no questions** add **-ഓ** (-ō) to the word being questioned — usually the verb: ആണ് → **ആണോ?** *āṇō?* 'is it?', അറിയാം → **അറിയാമോ?** 'do you know?'. Answer with ആണ്/അതെ ('yes, it is') or അല്ല ('no, it isn't').

dialogue.title: On the train to Thiruvananthapuram
dialogue.setting: Tom, a traveller, chats with Priya, a college student, on a train.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: My name is Tom. And yours?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: I'm Priya. Where are you from, Tom?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: ഞാൻ ഇംഗ്ലണ്ടിൽ നിന്നാണ്. ഇപ്പോൾ കൊച്ചിയിൽ താമസിക്കുന്നു.
lines.roman: ñān iṅglaṇḍil ninnāṇŭ. ippōḷ kocchiyil tāmasikkunnu.
lines.en: I'm from England. Now I live in Kochi.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: Really? Do you know Malayalam, Tom?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: A little. Where's your hometown, Priya?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: കൊള്ളാം! തൃശ്ശൂർ പൂരം വളരെ പ്രശസ്തമാണ്, അല്ലേ?
lines.roman: koḷḷām! Trushshūr pūram vaḷare prashastamāṇŭ, allē?
lines.en: Nice! The Thrissur Pooram festival is very famous, isn't it?

culture: Using someone's **name** instead of 'you' (ടോമിന് മലയാളം അറിയാമോ? 'Does Tom know Malayalam?') is a natural, polite way to talk to people your own age. Kerala has a huge diaspora, especially in the Gulf, so 'Where's your nāṭŭ?' (hometown) is often the first question two Malayalis ask each other abroad.
